article.title: Why a Small Sample Can Give a Big Surprise

paragraphs.en: A small sample can produce a result that looks dramatic even when the underlying population has not changed much. Imagine asking five customers whether they like a new service. If four say yes, the satisfaction rate is 80 percent. That sounds impressive, but one different answer would change the rate to 60 percent. With one thousand customers, a single answer barely moves the percentage. This is sampling variability. Small samples naturally move around more because each observation has a large influence. Rare outcomes make the problem stronger. If only a few purchases or claims occur, adding or losing one event can create a large relative change. Analysts should therefore look at the number of observations, the number of events, and uncertainty around the estimate rather than reading the percentage alone. A confidence interval can show that a small sample supports a wide range of plausible values. Repeating the measurement over time can also reveal whether an apparent jump persists. This does not mean small samples are useless. They can provide early signals and help teams learn what to investigate next. But they should not be presented with the same certainty as stable evidence from a large, well-designed sample. A good report says both what was observed and how much uncertainty remains. Numbers can look precise because they contain decimals, yet precision in formatting is not the same as precision in knowledge. Analysts should define the population, timing, comparison, and uncertainty before turning an observed pattern into a business conclusion.
